extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and readers of English poetry; poets and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles for reading, judging, or composing English (largely Romantic/early 19th-century) poetry: what counts as merit or fault in diction, feeling, structure, subject-choice, and effect on the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must act from real passions, not puppetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should speak and act from 'real passions of their own, or love either of virtue or vice' rather than as moral puppets manipulated to illustrate a moral title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt condemns playwrights who 'make moral puppets of them, pulls the wires, and they talk virtue and act vice, according to their cue and the title prefixed' (example: Miss Baillie). Anti-pattern: characters who exist only to demonstrate a labelled moral quality rather than to exhibit believable motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid insipid, sentimental 'baby-house theatricals'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry or drama that has an 'insipid and amiable' tone where 'virtue seems such a pretty playing at make-believe' should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that is excessively sweet, decorative, or designed to 'do-me-good' sacrifices truth and force. Hazlitt calls such work 'the perfection of baby-house theatricals'—pleasant but shallow and unconvincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of nature and simplicity of expression over decorative diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer truth of nature and simplicity to minute, far-fetched ornament; do not 'wrap up obvious thoughts in a glittering cover of fine words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Mr. Rogers: his verse is 'studiously inverted, and scrupulously far-fetched' so that 'you cannot see the thought for the ambiguity of the language, the figure for the finery.' Principle: diction should serve thought; avoid dazzling language that hides meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute elaborated poetic diction for substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry that is 'a tortuous, tottering, wriggling, fidgetty translation' of prose into fashionable poetical diction lacks truth and simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt compares bad ornamental poetry to a 'translation' into 'tantalizing, teasing, tripping, lisping' diction—an anti-pattern where style masquerades for content. Ensure ideas remain intelligible and forceful beneath any stylistic flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sense and logical coherence in phrasing and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not sacrifice sense and the 'keeping in the ideas' to a jingle of words or epigrammatic turns; metaphors/antitheses must make logical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Campbell's antithesis about a hamlet shade giving 'health in the breeze, and shelter in the storm' fails logically. Avoid 'curiosa infelicitas'—beautiful-sounding but nonsensical phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage: avoid excessive self-censorship and timidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets should not 'starve [their] genius to death' by excessive fear of critics; over-circumspection betrays talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt warns against 'maim[ing] and mangl[ing] ideas' to fit critics or 'playing the hypercritic on himself.' Principle for creators: be bold enough to allow thoughts to develop; anti-pattern is continual self-editing that kills originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical, contrived plotting and author-convenient coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in narrative or fable should arise naturally, not appear 'just in the nick of time' for the author's convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt criticises Campbell's reliance on systematic antitheses and a machine-like nature where the Indian 'vanishes and returns' as needed. Keep causal plausibility and organic development; contrivance undermines reader satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain intensity, momentum, and concentration of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Facility and excessive lightness of fancy can exhaust attention; poetry needs intensity and sustained force, not merely variety and brilliancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tom Moore's 'exuberance of involuntary power' and 'facility of production' make his work wear the reader out. Aim for concentrated force; avoid an inexhaustible but shallow profusion of small pleasures that dilute impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unify impressions into a coherent whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety should be subordinated to coherence—images and moments must connect into a whole rather than remain detached impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes Moore's images are 'detached, desultory, and physical'—they 'glance over the surfaces' instead of grappling with deep-rooted feelings. For larger poems, ensure unity and cumulative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos must be authentic, not mawkish or prettified
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiment should avoid 'mawkish sensibility' or crystallizing into 'all the prettinesses of allegorical language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moore's pathos 'sometimes melts into a mawkish sensibility.' Maintain sincerity and roughness of feeling where appropriate; avoid prettified, artificial tears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire and biting wit are valuable strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharpness of satire and 'wit at will' are high merits; where present they can be the author's best achievements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Moore's Twopenny Post-Bag as a 'perfect "nest of spicery"' and calls his satirical poetry 'first-rate.' Use satire to sharpen moral or social insight rather than merely ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dominating the work by a single, morbid mood or self-absorption
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitive obsession with one dark subject or the poet's own maladies risks making the work morbid and repulsive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Byron: the 'everlasting repetition of one subject' and 'unaccommodating selfishness' create a monotonous morbidness. Ensure variety of emotional register and that passion arises from wider engagement, not mere self-preying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects appropriate to poetic treatment (respect genre's suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subjects (e.g., historical/political figures) may be more proper for history than poetry; treat subjects with a consistent and appropriate poetic approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt objects to Byron's recurrent treatment of Buonaparte—writing alternately for and against him—as if the subject changed with the poet's humour. Principle: select subjects that reward poetic treatment and handle them consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial vividness is a virtue but not a substitute for moral/deep originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivid, picturesque description ('painterly' power) is valuable, but by itself it does not make a great poet if not joined to originality or moral depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walter Scott's 'clear, flowing, and transparent' style and 'picturesque power' make him popular, yet Hazlitt faults him for having 'no originality' and little moral force. Use pictorial skills to serve larger moral or imaginative aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to move and mould the reader, not merely entertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Great poetry should leave a determinate impression and 'mould the minds of others,' not just supply new 'images and associations' while leaving the reader unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt contrasts Scott's entertaining verse with the defining quality of a great mind. Strive for works that change the reader's perspective or feelings in a lasting way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality: draw from the poet's own mind and inner source
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry that is 'internal'—furnished from the poet's own mind and subject—has greater originality and significance than merely imitative or traditional verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Wordsworth as 'the most original poet now living' because he is his 'own subject.' Encourage inwardness and personal insight rather than fashion-driven imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive faculty for long forms: ensure movement and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer poems require machinery, constructive faculty, and forward movement; otherwise 'the poem stands stock-still.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt criticises Wordsworth's Excursion for lacking constructive drive—'the line labours, the sentiment moves slow, but the poem stands stock-still.' For longer works, plan progression, unity, and forward momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance natural simplicity with art and craft; avoid reactionary excess
rubrics_metrics.description: While valuing 'pure nature' and simplicity, do not discard all art, authority, or arrangement; simplicity should not become affected or outrageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt describes the Lake-school reaction against classical affectations and the resulting 'outrageous simplicity.' Principle: naturalness is good, but craft—measure, arrangement, and authority—remains essential; avoid simplistic revolt from all poetic technique.
